messages.subject: Critical Import Step?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all:

    While recently using DISTANCE 4.1, I was surprised by a few density =
outputs that seemed to be way off and out of line with other similar =
analyses.  After much consternation, I finally figured it out.  I was =
manipulating (sorting, filtering, etc.) the data in CSV format in MS =
Excel to produce several sub-files to simplify the import and analysis =
process.    In doing so, the columns that would eventually be labeled =
Region, Point Transect, or Line Transect were not in order.  And if a =
unique label (i.e. point transect) appeared several times and not in the =
same place (other labels were ahead and behind it in the order, before =
it appeared again), DISTANCE recognized the label as new, separate and =
unique.......even though the label is identical.   The result was a =
ridiculously low density output because the number of samples was =
(inappropriately) increased.  After re-organizing the data, the problem =
was corrected and the densities made sense (Effective Strip Width =
remained constant, however). =20
    So is it correct that data MUST be properly ordered at all times in =
the higher layers (everything above "observation") before importing it =
into DISTANCE?  This fundamental step may be widely known and embraced =
among most users.  Newer users such as myself that are digesting a lot =
of other procedures may, however, overlook it.   Especially if their =
data are only mildly out of order. =20

-Joel Jorgensen
University of Nebraska at Omaha

Hopefully this, and your posting, will help people avoid the same problems
you had.  The new help page will come out with the next release of Distance.

Hi Ioannis, list,

The only reason to import a shapefile into Distance currently is if you want
to do automated survey design.  In this case, you will need a shapefile for
the whole study area, to import into the global layer (and a shapefile for any
strata if you want to design by stratum).  The shapefile for the global layer
must consisit of one polygon, which you will attach to the single record in
the global layer of your Distance proejct (look in the Distance manual under
"importing existing GIS data").  It does not matter how many vertices
(corners) make up the polygon.  Hope this helps.  If you can't figure it out,
send me your shapefile and I'll have a look at it.

Cheers,

 - Len Thomas

P.S. I have recently added the ability to cut and paste the coordinates of
vertices from the Shape Properties Dialog, so that means it's possible (with
some effort) to import and export GIS data from other formats such as text
file.  This will be available in the next version of Distance.

messages.subject: Re: Covariates
messages.body_plain:
Hi Mike, List,

The issue of how to gather covariates for distance sampling can be
decomposed in 2: (1) which covariates to gather and (2) at what level to
gather them.

1. Which to gather

It is important to realize that the covariates are variables that you
believe influence the probability of detecting a butterfly (a common
mistake is to collect variables that affect animal density, but not its
detectability, to include in the detection function modeling - note
these might of course be useful, but they are not when modeling the
detection function; if you are planning to do any sort of spatial
modeling they might be important, but I'm assuming that is not the
primary objective here).

In that sense, something like say e.g. wind speed, temperature, cloud
cover, time of day, could be potentially interesting for you, because
these should all affect the butterflies activity, and hence their
detectability. If you have different observers, then observer is also a
possible one, because some observers might be better than others. You
can certainly think of other candidates - but you should not try to
collect all the possible covariates, because it is virtually impossible
to collect all those that affect detection - pooling robustness ensures
that you should be OK even if you miss some of these. The covariates
used should be independent of the distances themselves.

You mention nectaring plants. For example, percentage of nectaring
plants might be highly correlated to butterfly abundance, yet not be
related at all to the detection function. However, if the animals are
easyer to detect when over a given plant you might want to include a
covariate which is a yes/no typo of covariate - over plant / not over
plant. This reflects the fact that covariates can be either factors (say
background color) or non-factors (say temperature).

2. At what level

You can collect variables associated with diferent survey levels. Say
you had a species with two different color patterns, then color could be
a covariate, and this would be an observation level covariate. If you
want to collect say temperature, and do not want to collect a
temperature for each butterfly, but you take only around 10 minutes to
do a transect, you might collect temperature only once (say 5 minutes
after starting) and then all butterflies in that transect have the same
covariate value - it's a sample level covariate. The same holds true for
a strata level covariate. Distance treats these the same, because
ultimately the covariates are associated with each detection.

Hope this helps,

Tiago

messages.subject: Re: using covariates for density vs. detectability
messages.subject_clean: using covariates for density vs. detectability
messages.body_plain:
Hi Karen, list,

At its simplest, you just want Distance to estimate the density of the bird
species of interest at each point (ie density by sample).  You can then use
this as the response variable in a regression analysis, with your habitat
variables being the covariates predicting density.

However, there are plenty of complications that you might consider taking
account of.  I summarize some of them below, but there's really too many
issues here to be dealt with in a single email.  Most are dealt with in
Chapter 4 of Advanced Distance Sampling, although that mostly focusses on
line transects; there is definately a need for a straightforward paper
outlining the issues for point transects, which are rather simpler.  Also
note that we are currently adding this kind of functionality to Distance,
and will be teaching a workshop on it next summer.  Lastly, there is a paper
in Ecology by Royle et al. (2004, 85(6): 1591-1597) outlining a different
approach, which I don't think will work when detectability varies between
points (just my opinion however).

Some issues:

- In general one could include other covariates, such as location (lat, long
coordinates), etc

- Regression modelling might be done via a generalized linear or generalized
additive model, so you don't have to assume a normal distribution for the
response variable and you could include a smooth relationship between the
response variable and the covariates (the latter not relevant for you as you
don't have any continuous covariates)

- You could also use count as the response variable, and account for
variation in density by including an offset in the linear predictor for
effective area of the point.  However, can't get effective area when there
are animal-level covariates in the detection function (such as group size
for example).  Another possible response variable is estimated number of
animals in the point, rather than estimated density.

- Whatever the reponse variable, thought should be given to the error
distribution to use.  If the response variable is count or estimated number
of animals per point then a Poisson or negative binomial could be
considered.  If density, a normal or lognormal might work okay; or even
Poisson or negative binomial despite the non-discrete data.  Often there is
a problem with too many zeros, and unfortunately "standard" approaches
involving zero-inflated distributions do not work where probability of
detection is less than 1 (unpublished work by David Borchers).

- Another potential pitfall is lack of independence in the response variable
between points.  This occurs for two reasons: first, estimates of (say)
density are not independent between points as they share parameters of the
detection function.  Secondly, there may be residual pattern not accounted
for by the covariates (e.g., spatial clustering in density) that means the
residuals are correlated.  The second problem could potentially be solved
several ways (e.g., allowing spatial autocorrelation in the error term), but
the first is not so easy to find a straightforward solution to.  Lack of
independence tends to cause the model selection criteria (e.g., AIC) to lead
you to fit too many covarites (ie overfit) and also causes the analytic
variance estimate to be an underestimate.  A simple workaround for now is to
use common sense to avoid overfitting (ie be conservative in the choice of
covariates) and to use a resampling approach to variance estimation (e.g.,
bootstrap resampling with point as the replicate, fitting both the detection
function model and the density model within each replicate).

At present, my impression is that most people who are using distance-
sampling methods to model density as a function of covariates are ignoring
most of these problems, especially the lack of independence one.  Not ideal,
but trying to account for them currently requires quite substantial
statistical sophistication, and possibly the ability to program a boostrap
in some programming language and call Distance within each bootstrap
replicate.  As I said before, we're currently working on adding this kind of
facility to Distance, and expect to have that finished by early next summer
at the latest.  We're planning on teaching workshops on that stuff next
summer.  We are also working on a more long-term project to come up with
methods for density surface modelling that use less ad-hoc methods to
account for the lack of independence problem, and expect results from that
late in 2007.

Hope this helps,

 - Len

Dear list members,

I am interested in the effect of sheep grazing on density of high mountain
birds in Norway. To investigate this we have used a randomized block (east,
west and middle) design with enclosures with high sheep density, low sheep
density and controls. Each treatment has 3 replicates, i.e., we have
altogether 9 enclosures (called A to I). The size of each enclosure is ca
300 m x 1 km and they lie adjacent to each other. To get a measure of bird
density we traversed the enclosures along line transects. During each day
the full area was traversed 2-3 times =96 that is I got 2-3 line transect
segments per day from all 9 enclosures (6-9 segments if I pool in treatment
groups). Line transect from the same day were always sufficiently spatially
separated. Typically ca 50 birds were observed per day primarily consisting
of 5-6 common insectivorous species. Hence, the number of birds for each
line segment (within each enclosure) is very low. During the study period of=

1 month ca 1300 birds were recorded.=20

Question 1. What should I choose as my line transect unit?

In my first analysis attempt in Distance I used =93treatment=94 as region an=
d
transect per day per enclosure as line transect unit (i.e., I pooled 2-3
line segments per day). One problem here is that possible variation among
the three enclosures receiving the same treatment is not picked up. Also,
the sample size per line transect is now much fewer than Buckland et al's
60-80 recommended observations.

In a second attempt I continued to use =93treatment=94 as region and pooled =
all
transects per enclosure from the full study period. Now sample size per
transect line increase but the number of lines decrease to 3 per treatment.
Also I regard it is problematic to pool observations from a long time period=

like this.=20

Do you think the setup in my first analysis attempt is a good choice?

Question 2. How to incorporate a covariable which varies within line transec=
ts

The abundance of birds seams to be much higher in one habitat type than all
others. We have a GIS map with habitat types and we also recorded the
habitat type where the bird was observed in field. My problem is that
habitat types change within each line transect segment. Hence, we do not
have a stratified setup with good and bad habitat types, but must include it=

is a covariable in some way. I think habitat primarily affect overall
abundance but possibly also the shape of the detection function.=20

Do any of you have a suggestion on how to incorporate habitat in my analyses=
?=20
I am more familiar with the software R. If the detection function does not
differ among treatments, do you think I can analyse my bird observations as
a poisson process in R? That would simplify the analysis on the effect of
covariables for me.=20

I am extremely greatful for any hint to the above questions. Also, a
response on where to find the answers in books or the online distance manual=

is highly appreciated.=20

Barry (and Distance sampling list):

There have been a number of queries to this list about formatting
trapping web data for analysis in Program Distance.  The most recent
answer was provide by Dr. Thomas on 15 September of this year.
(http://www.jiscmail.ac.uk/cgi-bin/webadmin?A2=ind0509&L=DISTANCE-SAMPLING&P=R307&I=-3&X=4DBD493CEAC91402D7&Y=eri...%40mcs.st-and.ac.uk).

Entry of trapping web data is very similar to entry of point transect
data, as that is the method by which data are analysed to produce
density estimates.  There are 2 forms of inquiry that will be of
interest in getting entered into Distance:

1)  First, you should consult the sample projects that came with your
download of Distance.  Both the "house wren" and "songbird" sample
projects show data gathered from point transects, so their format are
applicable to the entry of trapping web data.  Note particularly the
recognition of no detections at a point transect (web) during a sampling
event.  This occurred on Point 5 of Region (stratum) 0 in the "house
wren" project, as well as Point 17 of Pasture 1 in 1980 in the
"songbird" project.  Note that there is no distance recorded associated
with the lack of detection (or capture).  Providing a distance of 0
implies an animal was detected at the sampling point (or centre of the
trapping web).  As you note, this has considerable significance for your
detection function.  You really, really, do not want to enter a distance
zero if nothing was detected.

2)  You will want to acquaint yourself with entering distances in
intervals (also know as binned data).  Data from the sample projects I
describe above are all continuous data (ungrouped).  However, as your
traps are laid in concentric rings, distances are not continuous, but
rather constrained to the number of rings of traps you laid out.
Consult p.94 (Chapter 8) of the Distance users guide for version 5 beta
4 for a discussion of entering binned data.

Barry:

I don't believe the concept of clusters applies with rodents captured in
a trapping web.  The animals were captured as individuals, not detected
as a herd of mice roaming across your study site.  There is no purpose
served by estimating cluster sizes of animals in this type of study.

data were collected as individuals, the data should be analysed in that
manner.  I can't fathom an advantage to treating the data as clusters;
do you have a reference for this method you describe?

Unless there is a compelling reason to treat the data in a manner
dissimilar to the manner in which they were collected, you should treat
the detections as individual observations.
